catalog_quote: Most of Omotic languages have either tone or pitch accent. ... In Dime tone has not been well treated in any of the previous studies. In the present study, we only treat the vital roles played by tone without discussing tone fully. Thus, the tone system in Dime needs further investigation. Dime has two basic tones, H and L, we represent high tone by ( ́) and leave low tone unmarked. The tone-bearing unit is the vowel; there are no tone-bearing consonants or syllabic nasals in the language. Within a syllable a long vowel or a diphthong may bear a contour tone. ... 2.4.1 Tone patterns in nouns and verbs. In this section we discuss monosyllabic words. All possible combinations of H and L tone occur on monosyllabic words. ... Otherwise the Dime lexicon is predominantly disyllabic. The following are examples of tone patterns in disyllabic nouns and verbs. ... LH wontsú 'answer' ... HH bínd…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal' (no word-stress rule; domain not stated by the source) rests on the standard and only reference grammar of Dime (Mulugeta Seyoum 2008, LOT 178), which we hold as publisher PDF + text; the deciding quotation and locator (sec. 2.4-2.4.2, pp. 29-31, fn. 13 = Fleming 1990:539) are confirmed verbatim, and a full-text search for stress/accent confirms the grammar never posits word stress — the only 'stress' mention is Fleming's sentence-final question-intonation remark, correctly recorded in the the domain quotation field. Glottolog lists no competing grammar or phonology; Crossref shows no JIPA Illustration or prosody article. The unheld items (Fleming 1990 sketch, SIL 2016 40-pp brief grammar, Azeb Amha 2012 overview) are older, shorter or secondary and could at most refine, not overturn, the classification. download log at
